note.S:
CC: A red sore patch on my left shin is getting bigger.

HPI: 42-year-old male. Expanding left shin erythema for 2 days. Began around anterior left shin scratch. Warmth and tenderness predominate over itch. 4/10; normal reported walking ability. Steady discomfort. Expanded from coin-sized to palm-sized. Gardening scratch; insect exposure without witnessed bite at site. Worse with touch and prolonged standing. Elevation relieves aching. Cleansed with soap/water; petrolatum only. No similar prior infection.

PMH: Bilateral varicose veins; no known diabetes or immunocompromise. Reported tetanus immunization 3 years ago.

PSH: No surgical/procedural history.

Meds: No regular medication or systemic steroids.

SH: Former smoker: 6 pack-years; quit 5 years ago. No alcohol. No recreational/injection drugs. Barber; prolonged standing. Partner can monitor skin changes.

FH: Mother: postoperative DVT; no known unprovoked familial thrombosis. Father: hypertension; sister: no known major illness.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

ROS: Skin: Localized shin erythema. No drainage. Initial mild itch; pain now predominant. General: No fever. No chills. No malaise. Cardiovascular: No chest pain. No dyspnea. Localized swelling; no whole-calf swelling.
note.O:
Vitals: BP 126/78 mmHg, P 84 bpm, R 16 rpm, T 99.0 F oral, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 6' 0", Wt 190 lbs

General: Well appearing and hemodynamically stable.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm without murmur.
Lungs: Clear bilateral breath sounds.
Skin: Anterior left shin: 8 by 10 cm poorly demarcated erythema surrounding a superficial scratch, without vesicles, bullae, necrosis or purulent drainage. Visible superficial varicosities.
Skin: Skin warm and tender without fluctuance, crepitus, pain beyond visible margins or a palpable venous cord.
Extremities: Mild localized edema at lesion; calves symmetric and nontender; capillary refill under 2 seconds.
Heart: Pedal pulses 2+ bilaterally.
Osteopathic: L2 left lumbar paraspinal tissue texture change and tenderness.
A: 2. Large local inflammatory reaction to an insect bite
P: 1. Mark the erythema margin and start an appropriate oral streptococcal-active antibiotic after clinician assessment; a 5-day course is reasonable if improving, adjusted to response/local guidance. Elevate, clean and protect the scratch; no routine culture or MRSA coverage without indication. Review in 48–72 hours. Rapid spread, disproportionate pain, fever or systemic illness needs urgent evaluation.

2. If reassessment supports a noninfectious bite reaction, emphasize cool compresses and appropriate antipruritic treatment rather than unnecessary antibiotics. Explain the difference between itch-predominant local inflammation and worsening infection; monitor the marked margin.

3. If cord-like tenderness, progression or DVT features appear, use venous ultrasound to define extent and assess deep involvement before selecting treatment. Discuss leg elevation and safe symptom relief; emergency evaluation is needed for new chest pain or breathlessness.

reasoning.question: Is the area spreading, is pain disproportionate, and is there pus or a venous cord?
reasoning.why: Describe a localized skin lesion and separate infection from inflammatory and venous mimics.
reasoning.if_present: Use the reported pattern to select the relevant examinations and assess urgency.
reasoning.if_absent: Keep alternatives open and ask a focused follow-up.
reasoning.document: Separate reported symptoms, observed signs, assessment and proposed care.

differentials.name: Nonpurulent cellulitis
differentials.teaching_context: Progressive warmth/tenderness around a skin break supports cellulitis without abscess or systemic illness.

differentials.name: Large local inflammatory reaction to an insect bite
aliases: Large local inflammatory reaction to an insect bite
differentials.teaching_context: Outdoor exposure and initial itching allow a bite reaction; progressive tenderness and a visible scratch favor cellulitis.

differentials.name: Superficial thrombophlebitis
differentials.teaching_context: Varicosities and focal painful erythema support consideration; absence of a cord and diffuse contact-area inflammation make it less likely.

omissions: Explaining uncertainty and the practical follow-up plan.
